channel.title: The Tomorrow Post
channel.description: A newspaper for the digital age. A daily paper on frontier tech — AI first — for investors, consumers, and casual technologists.

item.title: Malware Now Hands Stolen Data to an AI Model and Asks What the Victim Is Worth
item.description: Cisco Talos documented a Windows infostealer that, after taking passwords, cookies and payment cards, sends the haul to a commercial AI model with instructions to rank the victim's most valuable assets. If the first model refuses, the malware tries a second, then a third. Talos reports no evidence the malware has been used in real attacks.
item.content:encoded:
Cisco Talos published its analysis of a Windows infostealer it calls VOLTA on October 31. The theft side is conventional and thorough: browser credentials, cookies and saved payment cards from Chromium browsers, Firefox and Thunderbird; session tokens for Discord, Telegram, Steam and Roblox; Microsoft OAuth tokens; cryptocurrency wallet material; SSH and cloud configuration files; Wi-Fi profiles and screenshots. Talos says the malware then uses stolen access to enrich the haul, searching a victim's email for purchase receipts and pulling delivery histories.

The new part comes after the theft. VOLTA assembles the collected material into a structured bundle and, when it has an API key, sends it through OpenRouter to a commercial AI model. Its prompt tells the model to act as a forensic intelligence analyst drafting a target assessment, with sections headed 'WHAT THEY'RE WORTH' — valuables ranked by how easily they can be turned into money — and 'THEIR OPSEC,' an assessment of the victim's security habits. The default model is Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.6. The malware scans each reply for refusal phrases such as 'I can't,' and on a refusal falls back to Moonshot's Kimi K2 and then to Google's Gemini 2.5 Flash. The output is saved as a file named AI_Analysis.txt and exfiltrated with the rest.

Talos is explicit about the limits of the finding. The researchers, led by Ryan Fetterman, found VOLTA through CAIRN, a toolkit Talos open-sourced on September 22 for hunting malware with built-in AI. They have not reported whether any of the three models complied or refused in testing, and they have not tracked the malware in use in real attacks; the sample was first seen on October 11. Without a configured API key, the AI stage is skipped and VOLTA works as an ordinary stealer. The significance of the sample is the division of labor it assumes: the commodity part of an intrusion is no longer reading what was stolen, because a rented model will read it, rank it and write the summary.

item.title: Alibaba's Qwen Will Power Apple Intelligence in China, With Testing From November 4
item.description: Apple and Alibaba announced on Saturday that Qwen will supply the model behind Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence for iPhone users in China. Testing starts November 4 in the developer beta; the public release is planned for December. The rebuilt Siri assistant is not part of the package.
item.content:encoded:
Apple Intelligence is coming to iPhones in mainland China on a Chinese model. Apple announced on its China newsroom on Saturday that testing begins November 4 in the latest iOS developer beta, with a public release planned for December in iOS 27.3. Alibaba confirmed the partnership the same day: its Qwen models will be integrated into Siri, Writing Tools and Visual Intelligence, covering text and image understanding and content generation. Alibaba's chief executive, Eddie Wu, said Qwen would be deeply integrated across Apple's ecosystem.

The arrangement reflects the regulatory structure of the market. Generative AI services in China require local approval, and reporting on the announcement notes that China's cyberspace regulator registered Apple's on-device generative AI service in July. In China, Qwen stands in the position ChatGPT occupies elsewhere in Apple Intelligence: for certain requests, Siri can pass a question to Qwen and draw on its knowledge, and a Compose option in Writing Tools lets it draft original text. The integration is opt-in — users choose whether to enable it and what to share — and Alibaba says requests sent through Apple Intelligence, and the responses generated, will not be used to train its models.

What Chinese users are getting is the first generation of the product, two years after its United States launch. Apple's announcement states that the December release does not include Siri AI or the other next-generation Apple Intelligence features announced at its 2026 developers conference — the rebuilt assistant now rolling out elsewhere is not in this package. Eligibility is narrow: an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone bought in China, or a device whose location and Apple Account region are both set to China, with support for other Apple platforms to follow after further approvals. The first outside check on the arrangement arrives quickly: developers can test Qwen's behavior inside Siri and Writing Tools from Tuesday's beta.

item.title: Pope Leo XIV Asked States to Ban Lethal Autonomous Weapons at November Talks in Geneva
item.description: Addressing AI researchers at the Vatican on Friday, Pope Leo XIV said decisions over human life and the use of force must remain under human control, rejected legal personhood for AI systems, and urged states meeting in Geneva in November toward a prohibition of lethal autonomous weapons.
item.content:encoded:
Pope Leo XIV used an address to AI researchers at the Vatican on Friday, October 30, to ask states meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward prohibiting lethal autonomous weapons. Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force, he said, must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human control, and artificial intelligence must be 'disarmed.' The meeting — 'The Future of AI: A Dialogue between the Vatican and the Scientific World' — was organized by the Pontifical Academy for Life and the Future of Life Institute.

The address restated the position of his May encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas, in five considerations, and drew a line his predecessor also drew: Pope Francis told the G7 in 2024 that no machine should ever choose to take a human life. Leo rejected proposals to grant AI systems legal personhood — 'Machines are instruments, not people' — arguing that responsibility for a system's actions rests with its human creators and operators, and called for shared international standards, independent oversight and clear mechanisms of accountability. The remarks are a moral appeal to negotiators, not law; no state has committed to the ban ahead of the Geneva talks. In a separate note of the same week, the Holy See Press Office confirmed that the Pope, who was born in Chicago, has already mailed his ballot for Tuesday's United States midterm elections.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Permission Is Now a Line Item
item.description: A judge held that the turbines powering xAI's Colossus site are not exempt from air permits, so whether they were ever permitted will be argued in full. The ruling decides no liability — and that is the point: permission has moved from a filing made before construction to a legal exposure carried during operation.
item.content:encoded: A data center used to need land, power and capital. The ruling in Mississippi adds a fourth requirement in a form builders cannot schedule around: a judge held that the turbines powering xAI's Colossus site are not exempt from air permits, so the question of whether they were ever permitted will be argued in full. The ruling decides no liability, and that is the point. Permission has moved from a filing made before construction to a legal exposure carried during operation, at a cost counted in time and in public. October's scarcest input was a grid connection. November's may be consent.

item.title: The New York City Marathon Runs Its 50th Five-Borough Race Today
item.description: The TCS New York City Marathon runs today on the 50th anniversary of its five-borough course, with both defending champions — Benson Kipruto, who won last year by three hundredths of a second, and Hellen Obiri, the women's course-record holder — and an extra hour in the morning, returned by the overnight clock change.
item.content:encoded:
The TCS New York City Marathon runs today, Sunday, November 1, on the 50th anniversary of the race's five-borough course. The professional women start at 8:35 a.m. Eastern and the professional men at 9:05 a.m., on a morning made longer by the calendar: clocks went back one hour at 2 a.m., so the race's early waves start on the extra hour the fall change returns.

Both defending champions are back. Benson Kipruto of Kenya won the men's race last year by three hundredths of a second over Alexander Mutiso — the closest finish in the race's history — and Hellen Obiri returns after setting the women's course record of 2:19:51 last November. Obiri's challengers include Sheila Chepkirui, the 2024 champion, and Edna Kiplagat, who won in 2010. Two expected contenders are absent: Olympic champion Sifan Hassan withdrew after illness disrupted her preparation, and American Fiona O'Keeffe is out with an injury. The American men's race pairs Conner Mantz, the national record holder at 2:04:43, against Zouhair Talbi, whose 2:03:45 in Boston in April is the fastest marathon run by an American, on a course not eligible for records.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: A Federal Judge Let the Lawsuit Over xAI's Data Center Turbines Proceed
item.description: A federal judge denied xAI's request to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit over the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis. The court rejected the company's argument that the turbines are mobile equipment exempt from air permits. The ruling decides no liability; it means the permit question will now be heard in full.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge has denied xAI's motion to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit over the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis, TechCrunch reported on Saturday. Judge Debra M. Brown of the US District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi ruled that the plaintiffs have standing under the Clean Air Act, that the turbines are not 'mobile sources' under Mississippi's state implementation plan, and that the Act's citizen-suit provision does not violate the Constitution. The ruling, released on Friday, October 30, allows the case to proceed. It does not decide whether xAI violated the Act.

What the suit alleges

The NAACP and the Mississippi State Conference of the NAACP filed the case on April 14, 2026, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center. The center says xAI 'installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.' The complaint in the Mississippi case, as summarized in Saturday's coverage, alleges that X.AI Corp. and MZX Tech LLC installed and operated 27 gas turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, from August to December 2025 without an air permit, and that the turbines powered AI data centers in the Memphis area and emitted smog-forming pollutants and particulate matter. xAI's defense was procedural: the turbines are mobile, and therefore exempt; the plaintiffs lack standing; and citizen suits of this kind are unconstitutional. The court rejected each argument at this stage.

The second ruling in a month

This is the second dismissal attempt the case has survived in October. On October 19, the same court allowed the federal government to intervene in the case while denying its request to end it. Abre' Connor, the NAACP's director of environmental and climate justice, described Saturday's outcome as 'another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.' xAI is now owned by SpaceX; the company has not, in the reporting, answered the underlying allegation — whether the permits were required and were not obtained.

The case lands inside a thread this paper has followed since its first edition: the buildout's binding constraint is power, and power is obtained in public. Edition 001's lead was a data center abandoned for want of a grid connection; Edition 005 recorded moratoria, grid queues and local opposition delaying projects. The Colossus ruling is the courtroom version of the same constraint. A builder can install turbines faster than a grid connection can be approved; what Saturday's ruling establishes is that the speed does not settle the permission, and that the permission question can be litigated while the machines run.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: The First Known Fruit-Eating Dinosaur Had Chewing Muscles Built Like a Parrot’s
item.description: A small Cretaceous dinosaur, Infernogallus jamesi, had a chewing-muscle arrangement seen today only in fruit-eating parrots — evidence that some dinosaurs ate fruit, and may have carried the seeds that spread flowering plants.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.

item.title: Colorectal Cancer in Patients Under 50 Is Biologically Different, a 189-Tumor Study Finds
item.description: Tumors from patients diagnosed before 50 carry proportionally more stromal cells and fewer epithelial cells than tumors from older patients, in the largest study of its kind — a possible reason the disease behaves more aggressively in younger people.

item.title: AI-Designed Virus Shells Delivered Genes to Primate Brains 152 Times Better
item.description: Dyno Therapeutics’ engineered capsids reached the brain far more efficiently than the standard AAV9 in non-human primates, and versions built to evade antibodies tested negative against up to 85% of human serum samples. All of it is preclinical.

item.title: Crushed Shells Mixed Into Beach Sand Helped Young Clams Grow in More Acidic Water
item.description: Adding shell fragments to the sand where baby clams burrow changed the water between the grains, lowered its acidity, and produced larger shells — a measured version of a shell-adding practice Indigenous communities have used for generations.

item.title: The Clocks Went Back at 2 A.M., on the Earliest Date the Change Can Fall
item.description: Daylight saving time ended at 2 a.m. this morning, the earliest date the fall change can occur. The House voted in July to make daylight saving permanent; the Senate has not acted, so the 25-hour day proceeded on schedule.
item.content:encoded:
Daylight saving time ended at 2 a.m. local time this morning, Sunday, November 1, when clocks across most of the United States went back one hour to 1 a.m. — making today a 25-hour day and this the earliest date on which the fall change can fall, since the rule sets it on the first Sunday in November. Sunrise and sunset both arrive about an hour earlier by the clock from today: brighter mornings, darker evenings, until daylight saving returns on March 14, 2027.

The change happened under a law Congress nearly replaced this year. The Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent and end the twice-yearly switch, passed the House of Representatives in July and has not been taken up by the Senate, which is in an extended election recess — so the ritual proceeded on its 2007 schedule. Hawaii and most of Arizona do not observe daylight saving time and did not change their clocks. The overlap that made this weekend unusual — Halloween on Saturday followed immediately by the fall-back — last occurred in 2020 and, by the calendar's arithmetic, will not happen again until 2037.

item.title: Chainalysis Said an Attacker Using AI Agents Accessed Customer Names, Emails and Roles
item.description: Chainalysis, whose software traces cryptocurrency crime for law enforcement and exchanges, disclosed on Friday that an attacker used AI agents to reach its internal systems earlier in October. Names, email addresses, user IDs and organization role labels were accessed. The company reports no evidence that investigation content, credentials or session tokens were reached.
item.content:encoded:
Chainalysis disclosed on Friday that an external attacker used what the company calls 'offensive agentic techniques' to gain unauthorized access to its systems and internal tools earlier in October. The data accessed was customer identity information: user IDs, full names, email addresses and organization role labels for users provisioned on its platform. Chainalysis said its investigation to date has found no evidence of unauthorized access to investigation content, authentication credentials or session tokens, and that it is still determining which records were accessed for each organization.

The company's business is tracing other people's breaches. Chainalysis sells blockchain analytics to law enforcement agencies, government bodies, exchanges and financial institutions, which makes the accessed directory — who works on crypto investigations, at which organization, in what role — the sensitive part of an incident the company describes as involving non-sensitive data. Chainalysis said it is patching vulnerabilities and hardening its systems, is working with external cybersecurity experts, and is using large language models to support a broader security review. It advised customers to enable two-factor authentication and to watch for impersonation attempts.

Chainalysis stated that the incident is not related to the theft of about $6.3 billion from the exchange Binance, reported in Edition 013. The disclosure does not say which vulnerabilities were exploited, which internal tools were reached, or how long the attacker was inside; 'offensive agentic techniques' is the company's description, and it offered no detail on the methods. What is established is narrower than the phrase suggests: an attacker used AI tooling of some kind, and the firm that tracks crypto crime is now in the position of its own customers — disclosing an intrusion whose full scope is still being determined.

item.title: Cells Can Now Record What They Were Doing Days Ago
item.description: Engineered organelles archive a cell’s own RNA as it works — so days later, researchers can read back which genes were active, including in the rare cancer cells that survive chemotherapy and seed relapse.

item.title: A Structure Called the Cat’s Tail Records a Pluto-Scale Collision 63 Light-Years Away
item.description: Hubble has imaged the Cat’s Tail in visible light for the first time: a dark stream about 1,000 times the Earth–Sun distance across, inside a young star’s debris disk — evidence of a collision between bodies the size of Pluto.

item.title: The Buildout Now Needs Permission
item.description: This paper's first edition argued the scarcest asset in AI is a signed grid connection. A year of reporting later, the constraint has a second form: courts, permits and public consent. A federal ruling in Mississippi, polling that shows most Americans opposed to new data centers, and a Google chip answering prompts from orbit are three points on the same line.
item.content:encoded:
The Tomorrow Post's first edition, on October 19, led with a sentence that has organized a year of reporting: the scarcest asset in AI may be a signed grid connection. The evidence since has widened the point. Edition 005 recorded the buildout meeting zoning boards — moratoria in several states, grid queues, and projects cancelled when power could not be delivered on any useful schedule. On Friday, a federal judge in Mississippi added the courtroom to the list of places where a data center's power supply is decided, denying xAI's motion to dismiss the NAACP's Clean Air Act suit over the Colossus turbines and rejecting the argument that a turbine on a trailer is not a source of pollution the law reaches.

The public side of the same constraint is measurable. Polling summarized in weekend coverage of the buildout's finances puts opposition to new data centers at about two-thirds of Americans, with disputes over electricity prices, environmental effects and jobs named as the drivers. Opposition at that level does not stop projects by itself; it changes their timelines and their politics, which for a financed project is the same as changing their cost. The week also supplied the scale of what is being consented to: an account of the five largest builders' latest filings put their combined quarterly spending on property and equipment about $31.8 billion above what their operations brought in — arithmetic from the companies' 10-Q reports, reported Saturday. Every one of those dollars assumes a site where building is allowed to proceed.

Against that background, the weekend's most quietly significant item was a poem. On October 30, Google said its Project Suncatcher prototype satellite had returned the first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit: its Gemma 4 model, loaded before launch, answered a prompt with a haiku — 'Blue marble below / Data streams in silent grace / Starlight feeds my core' — downlinked as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway. The satellite, built with Planet and launched October 1 on a SpaceX rideshare, carries four TPUs and generates up to 1 kilowatt; only one chip can run at a time, for about twenty minutes. Google gives no performance figures, and the tests that matter — heat and radiation — come next, ahead of two interconnected satellites planned for 2027.

Read together, the three items describe one industry at three distances from the same problem. On the ground, compute needs permission: permits, courts and neighbors now sit inside the critical path alongside chips and capital, and a ruling like Friday's reprices time itself. In the polling, the public whose electricity bills and land carry the buildout is registering its answer before most projects reach it. In orbit, the largest builders are spending real money to learn whether the permission problem can be left behind entirely — at 1 kilowatt and twenty minutes at a time, which is to say: not yet, and not soon. The grid said no in October 2025. In November 2026 the answer is coming from more directions, and the builders are answering in more places.

item.title: Bleu Robotics Raised €5 Million to Teach Factory Humanoids a New Task From About Ten Demonstrations
item.description: The Paris startup, founded by two INRIA research directors and a former Renault assembly-line manager, says its software lets a humanoid robot learn a factory task from as few as ten operator demonstrations. Its stated target is full deployment on a production line in under an hour. The two industrial partners it cites are unnamed.
item.content:encoded:
Bleu Robotics, a Paris startup founded in 2025, has closed a €5 million pre-seed round co-led by Contrarian Ventures and OVNI Capital, with Kvanted, WEPA Ventures, Motier Ventures and Charlie Songhurst participating. The founding team combines research and factory experience: Jean-Baptiste Mouret and Serena Ivaldi are research directors at INRIA, the French national computing institute, with more than fifteen years in AI and robotics between them, and Benoît Berkoukchi managed assembly lines at Renault.

The company's claim is about setup time. Humanoid robots are general in form and specific in practice: each new factory task has traditionally meant weeks of programming and integration. Bleu says its learning system — it calls the method abductive learning — lets a humanoid learn a new task from as few as ten demonstrations by a human operator, and that it is targeting full deployment on a production line in one hour or less, at the accuracy above 99% that factories require. Those are the company's figures and goals, stated in its announcement coverage; they have not been independently tested. Bleu says it is already working with two major industrial companies and building partnerships with robot distributors; it does not name the companies.

The target customer explains the pitch. High-mix, low-volume manufacturers change tasks too often for conventional industrial robots, which repay their setup cost only across long identical runs. A humanoid that can be retaught in an hour would fit the work those factories actually have — if the demonstrated learning survives contact with a real line: varied parts, worn fixtures, and the accuracy standard the company itself cites. The pre-seed buys the test. What would settle the claim is a named customer reporting a deployment time, and that figure does not yet exist in public.

item.title: Starving Ants Protect Their Brains’ Energy First, Like Humans Do
item.description: When food runs short, ants keep supplying their brains at a rate comparable to the share humans protect — even though a colony is supposed to put the group ahead of any individual.

item.title: Anthropic Extended Its Text Watermark to Four More Claude Models, and One Setting Change Removes It on Two of Them
item.description: Anthropic is adding its invisible text watermark to Mythos 5, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 ahead of a European deadline. On Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 the mark applies only at default sampling settings, and Anthropic's own advice to customers who rely on it for compliance is to keep those defaults.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is extending its text watermark to four more Claude models — Mythos 5, Opus 4.7, Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 — in an email to API customers reported by The Decoder on Saturday. Newer models, including Opus 5.5, already carry the mark. The watermark is not a label attached to the text; Anthropic describes it as an imperceptible pattern in word choice, a variant of Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text method, which biases word selection during generation so the output carries a statistical signal that can be checked later. It adds no tokens, does not change pricing, and cannot be switched off. A detection API is in private preview.

On two of the four models, the mark has a condition. On Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6, it applies only when the three sampling parameters — temperature, top_p and top_k, which control randomness in word choice — are left at their defaults. Changing any one of them is enough to receive unmarked output. Anthropic's email states the condition plainly and warns customers: 'If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults.' The email carries no such caveat for Mythos 5 or Opus 4.7, which The Decoder reads as meaning the mark applies to those models at any settings.

The reason for the retrofit is a deadline. Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December transparency deadline: models released after August 2, 2026 shipped with the watermark from launch, and older models are being brought in in stages. The result is a compliance tool whose coverage depends, on two widely used models, on a configuration choice most developers make for unrelated reasons — output randomness. Anyone building a process on the assumption that Claude output is marked now has a documented exception to design around, published by the company itself.

item.title: Anthropic Took 66% of the Money and 48% of the Tokens in OpenRouter's Latest Week
item.description: In the most recent week of OpenRouter's data, Anthropic and OpenAI served nearly the same number of tokens and took very different shares of the spending: 48% of the tokens and 66% of the money for Anthropic, against 52% and 34% for OpenAI. The figures cover one routing platform, not the market.
item.content:encoded:
Peter Walker, OpenRouter's head of insights, posted the routing platform's chart of Anthropic's and OpenAI's 2026 usage on Saturday, under the summary 'Opus 5.5 reversed the trend.' In the most recent week on the chart, the two laboratories split the traffic almost evenly — Anthropic took 48% of the tokens routed between them and OpenAI 52% — and split the money unevenly: Anthropic took 66% of the spend and OpenAI 34%. The ratio between those shares works out to about 2.1 times as much spend per token for Anthropic as for OpenAI, by the arithmetic of FourWeekMBA's account of the chart.

The chart's totals give the scale. Tokens routed between the two laboratories have risen 224 times since the first week of 2026, and spend 81 times — which means the average price of a routed token has fallen by roughly two-thirds over the year, on the same arithmetic. Walker's account of the year has three moves: OpenAI regained spend share steadily, token volumes jumped with new low-cost models from both laboratories, and the launch of Opus 5.5 on September 22 reversed the spend trend back toward Anthropic. This paper reported on October 25 that Anthropic's token volume on OpenRouter rose about 3.6 times in the weeks after Opus 5.5 launched (Edition 006).

The limits of the data matter as much as the figures. OpenRouter is one routing platform, used disproportionately by developers rather than by the enterprise accounts both laboratories sell to directly, and a share of routed tokens is not a share of revenue. What the chart does establish is a price structure: at the layer where buyers can switch models with a line of code, the two frontier laboratories currently sell similar volumes of tokens at dissimilar prices, and the higher-priced one has been gaining since its September launch. Anthropic's roadshow, in the week of November 9, will ask public investors to price that structure.

item.title: A 237-Million-Year-Old Amphibian Appears to Have Lived Its Whole Life in the Ocean
item.description: No amphibian lives in the sea today. Chemical signatures in two armored fossils found in China match seawater, not the local rock — evidence of a marine amphibian 30 kilometers from the nearest possible island.

item.title: Starbucks' US Sales Rose 7.7%, on Bigger Tickets, Its Strongest Fall Menu, and 250 Closed Stores
item.description: Starbucks reported US comparable sales up 7.7% in its fiscal fourth quarter — ticket size up 5.2% and transactions up 2.4%. Its fall menu launch was the strongest in the company's history, matcha is now a $1 billion line, and about 250 closed stores contributed roughly two points of the growth as their customers moved.
item.content:encoded:
Starbucks' US same-store sales rose 7.7% in its fiscal fourth quarter, the company reported on Thursday — a 5.2% increase in average ticket and 2.4% growth in transactions, according to its earnings release, covered by Restaurant Dive. Global comparable sales rose 7.2%. Adjusted earnings were 80 cents a share, above the 72 cents analysts expected; revenue fell 4% to $9.14 billion, below the $9.2 billion expected, because the company converted its China retail operations to a licensed joint venture, which changed how that revenue is reported (Associated Press). Chief executive Brian Niccol said the chain is moving from turnaround to a sustained growth plan, with sales growth broad-based across income levels, generations and dayparts.

Two details in the quarter explain where the growth came from. The fall menu launch — headlined, as every year, by the Pumpkin Spice Latte — was the strongest fall deployment in the company's history, and matcha has grown into a $1 billion product line of its own, drunk mainly in the afternoon. And about 200 basis points of the comparable-sales growth came from store closures: Starbucks closed about 250 underperforming North American coffeehouses concentrated at the end of September, and their customers shifted to the stores that remained, chief financial officer Catherine Smith told analysts. For fiscal 2027, the company expects North American comparable sales to grow about 4%, and Smith said any price increases will remain focused and well below the Consumer Price Index. The shares fell almost 2% in after-hours trading on Thursday.

item.title: The Price Held. The Amount Did Not.
item.description: OpenAI kept the number that will be quoted, a $1.25 trillion valuation, and reduced the number that will be paid: a $20 billion target, a first close expected below it, and less than half of the original $30 billion raised, the Wall Street Journal reports. The first market-set price for a frontier lab now belongs to Anthropic's November roadshow.
item.content:encoded: OpenAI kept the number that will be quoted, a $1.25 trillion valuation, and reduced the number that will be paid. The target is now $20 billion, the first close is expected below that, and the Wall Street Journal reports less than half of the original $30 billion was raised. A private valuation is a negotiated figure, and the negotiation shows its limit: the price held because the amount gave way. The first market-set price for a frontier lab now belongs to Anthropic, whose roadshow starts in the week of November 9. Until that price exists, private valuations in this sector should be read with the condition Friday attached to this one: they hold for the amount investors will actually fund.

item.title: Polynesia’s Genomes Hold Drug Clues the Big Databases Missed
item.description: Genomes from more than 1,000 French Polynesians show founder effects at least ten times stronger than Finland’s — concentrating rare variants until their effects on health become measurable.

item.title: Polymarket Suspended International Trading After $2.6 Million Was Drained From User Accounts
item.description: Polymarket suspended international trading on Thursday after hackers drained more than $2.6 million from user accounts, CoinDesk reported — the second crypto security incident of the day, days before the midterm elections that bring prediction markets their largest audiences.
item.content:encoded:
Polymarket, the prediction-market platform, suspended international trading on Thursday after hackers drained more than $2.6 million from user accounts, CoinDesk reported on Friday. The suspension was the second crypto security incident reported on Thursday: the larger one, a $6.3 billion theft from the exchange Binance, is covered in this edition's Latest. CoinDesk's report gives the amount taken and the suspension; it does not describe how the accounts were accessed.

The timing is the part users will notice. Prediction markets take their largest public audiences in election weeks, and the US midterm elections are on Tuesday, November 3. A platform that suspends international trading days before that vote is removing, for its non-US users, the product at the moment of its highest demand — while its federally regulated rival Kalshi, covered in this edition, spent the same week raising $1 billion at a $40 billion valuation. Two platforms selling the same underlying product, event contracts, carried two different risks into election week: one regulatory and financial, one a security failure measured, so far, in single millions rather than billions.

item.title: OpenAI Cut Its Funding Target From $30 Billion to $20 Billion at a $1.25 Trillion Valuation
item.description: OpenAI cut the target for its bridge financing by a third on the day investor commitments were due, the Financial Times reported on Friday. The $1.25 trillion valuation stayed where the October talks had put it. The first close is expected to raise less than the new $20 billion target, and the Wall Street Journal reported that less than half of the original $30 billion had been raised.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI has cut the target for its new funding round from up to $30 billion to about $20 billion, the Financial Times reported on Friday, in a report carried by Reuters. The valuation is unchanged in this step at $1.25 trillion before new money. OpenAI set Friday, October 30, as the deadline for investors to commit. According to the Reuters account of the FT report, some investors reduced their allocations, and the first close of the round is expected to raise less than $20 billion. The account does not name the investors who cut back. OpenAI did not immediately respond to Reuters' request for comment. Later on Friday, the Wall Street Journal reported that OpenAI has raised less than half of its original $30 billion target in the round.

Who is in the smaller round

The FT reported that a consortium of investors from the United Arab Emirates, including the state-backed fund MGX, is expected to be the largest participant, and that under the arrangement OpenAI would gain an option to lease newly developed computing capacity in the region. Founders Fund, Coatue, Sequoia Capital and Andreessen Horowitz are also expected to participate, according to the FT report. Wealthy individuals are expected to be offered a subsequent retail offering at the same $1.25 trillion valuation. Those participation details are reported, not announced; OpenAI has made no statement about the round.

The round's path, on this paper's record

The financing has been repriced twice in five weeks. OpenAI first pitched a $1.4 trillion valuation (Edition 003). On October 22, CNBC and Bloomberg reported the valuation in talks at $1.25 trillion with up to $30 billion still sought, led by Coatue and UAE investors (Edition 003–004). Signatures were then targeted for Friday, October 30 (Editions 004–012), with some backers wanting Anthropic priced first (Edition 007) — a sequence that could not happen, since Anthropic's roadshow is scheduled for the week of November 9 (Edition 008). Friday's report resolves the collision by reducing the amount instead of waiting for the rival's price. OpenAI's last completed round, closed March 31, 2026, raised $122 billion in committed capital at an $852 billion post-money valuation, anchored by Amazon, Nvidia and SoftBank, according to the published accounts carried in Friday's coverage. The new round is described in that coverage as interim funding — a bridge toward a planned listing in the first half of 2027.

The cut landed on the week's hardest day for the sector's public prices. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% on Friday (see Latest), and after the close S&P Global Ratings turned its outlook on Meta negative, citing uncertainty over how long Meta's heavy capital spending will last, according to a summary of the action. Anthropic's roadshow, in the week of November 9, will now produce the first price for a frontier lab that a public market has set. OpenAI's $1.25 trillion remains a negotiated figure: agreed for the smaller amount investors funded on Friday, and untested at the $30 billion size at which it was first offered.

item.title: October Ended With the Bill Marked in Public
item.description: The month that opened with a $1.4 trillion pitch closed with three public tests of what AI claims are worth: a private round that defended its price by shrinking its size, an earnings season that marked down named balance sheets one at a time, and a $6.3 billion theft absorbed by a promise to cover it.
item.content:encoded:
October opened, on this paper's record, with a pitch: OpenAI seeking $1.4 trillion (Edition 003). It closed on Friday with three separate tests of what claims on the AI buildout are worth, each run in a different venue. In the private market, OpenAI defended the $1.25 trillion valuation its talks had settled on and cut the amount from $30 billion to $20 billion, with less than that expected at the first close (the Lead). In the public market, an earnings season that established demand — Azure up 48%, Google Cloud up 103%, AWS up 39% (Editions 011–012) — ended with the cash-flow test applied across the chip sector at once: Intel down 28.58% on guidance, the Nasdaq down 2.86% on the day and 5.3% on the month, while six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose (see Latest). In crypto, a $6.3 billion theft from the largest exchange was met with a freeze of about half the assets and a pledge to cover the rest, and bitcoin, after falling to $76,400, ended the day above $76,700.

Read together, the three tests drew the same line in three places. What held was the price attached to the established thing: OpenAI's valuation, the wider stock index, the value of a bitcoin. What gave way was the quantity attached to the promise: the size of the round funded on Friday, the fourth-quarter revenue Intel would commit to, the share of the stolen assets that could actually be frozen. October's repricing, in other words, has not been a repricing of the present. Demand for cloud capacity printed at record levels all month, the memory suppliers' order books sold out into 2027, and 82% of reporting S&P 500 companies beat estimates. The repricing has been applied to the next tranche — the unfunded part of every plan.

The financing record shows the same split from the lenders' side. Alphabet raised $147.2 billion from outside investors in the first nine months of the year (Edition 011). Amazon's long-term debt reached $173.1 billion (Edition 012). After Friday's close, S&P Global Ratings moved its outlook on Meta — which priced a $97.5 billion equity program on Tuesday (Edition 009) — to negative, citing uncertainty about how long the heavy spending lasts. None of those facts establishes that the spending fails. They establish that each new layer of it is being examined separately, at its own price, rather than carried on the strength of the layers beneath it. Two-tier money (Edition 007) has become the ordinary condition, not the warning.

November supplies the missing benchmark. On Monday, Apple and Palantir report, testing whether Friday's selloff stays inside the chip supply chain. On Tuesday, the midterm elections price the political environment the buildout's permits, power contracts and export rules will be written in. By Wednesday, Moonshot's Kimi weights are due — an open test of whether the frontier's capability claims can be checked by anyone with the file. And in the week of November 9, Anthropic's roadshow sets the first public price for a frontier lab, against a filed prospectus whose figures the market has now had two weeks to read. Every private number in this sector, including Friday's defended $1.25 trillion, will be quoted against that price from then on.

item.title: The Nasdaq Fell 2.86% on Friday, and Intel Fell 28.6% in Its Worst Day Since the 1970s
item.description: The Nasdaq Composite fell 747.72 points to 25,437.00 and the S&P 500 fell 1.82% in its worst session since June, as Intel fell 28.58% a day after guiding the fourth quarter below expectations. The selling stayed inside the chip sector: six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose, and the 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93%.
item.content:encoded:
US stocks closed sharply lower on Friday, October 30. The Nasdaq Composite fell 747.72 points, or 2.86%, to 25,437.00 — its lowest finish since July 31 — the S&P 500 lost 140.32 points, or 1.82%, to 7,580.07 in its worst session since June, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 572.25 points, or 1.09%, to 51,770.31 (Market Briefer, from exchange close reports). Intel fell 28.58% to $65.76, in what CNBC described as its worst session since the 1970s, a day after its fourth-quarter guidance came in below expectations (Edition 012). The semiconductor selloff took the Nasdaq 100 down 3.46% and a large semiconductor ETF down more than 8%; Qualcomm fell 11.12%, Nvidia fell 4.22%, Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell fell by double digits, and Broadcom and Micron each lost more than 5%. Technology was the S&P 500's weakest sector, down 4.24%. Amazon, which also reported Thursday night, fell 1.41%.

Outside the chip sector, the session was orderly. Six of the S&P 500's eleven sectors rose, led by energy, up 1.91%, and consumer staples, up 1.38%; utilities, health care, real estate and materials also finished higher. The Russell 2000 fell 1.66% to 2,811.84, and the Cboe Volatility Index rose to 19.42. The 10-year Treasury yield eased to 4.93% from 4.98%, ending October down roughly 36 basis points — its largest monthly decline since December 2023, according to the Wall Street Journal, as reported by Market Briefer. Gold fell 3.63% to $3,884.90 an ounce, its lowest level in about a year. The morning's labor data added nothing to either case: the third-quarter Employment Cost Index rose 0.8%, in line with expectations (Bureau of Labor Statistics). Of the 299 S&P 500 companies that had reported third-quarter results through Friday, 82% beat consensus estimates, according to LSEG data cited by Reuters.

For the month, the Nasdaq fell 5.3% — its largest monthly decline since March 2025 — and now sits more than 8% below its record closing high of October 6. The S&P 500 fell 0.9% in October while the Dow added 1.7%. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq have now fallen for three straight weeks. Friday's session applied, to the whole chip sector at once, the test Thursday's session had applied to Alphabet alone (Edition 012): earnings that beat estimates did not protect a company whose outlook showed the spending continuing. The difference on Friday is that the test had a named trigger — one company's guidance — and the rest of the market, and the bond market, declined to follow it.

item.title: A Molecular Brake Slows a Spinning Rotor 300,000-Fold
item.description: Researchers in Prague used light to block a molecular rotor’s spin. At very low temperatures, the braked rotor would need about 350 billion years for a single turn — roughly 25 times the age of the universe.

item.title: A Personal Vaccine Cut Melanoma Recurrence or Death Risk by 42% in a Phase 3 Trial
item.description: A vaccine built from each patient’s own tumor, added to immunotherapy after surgery, reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42% in 1,137 people with advanced melanoma. The result was reported at a European oncology meeting.

item.title: Kalshi Raised $1 Billion at a $40 Billion Valuation, Its Second $1 Billion Round in Five Months
item.description: Kalshi, the federally regulated prediction-market exchange, closed a $1 billion Series G co-led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital at a $40 billion post-money valuation. The company says annualized trading volume exceeds $1 trillion. Its sports contracts remain under legal challenge from state authorities.
item.content:encoded:
Kalshi announced a $1 billion Series G financing on October 29, in a company post reported by Crunchbase News on October 30. The round was co-led by Wellington Management and Sequoia Capital and values the company at $40 billion after the new money. Other participants include Baillie Gifford, Stripes, Andreessen Horowitz, Coatue, Layer Global, Morgan Stanley Investment Management, Sequoia Global Equities, CapitalG, Hudson River Trading and Balyasny Asset Management. The round follows a $1 billion raise about five months earlier at a $22 billion valuation.

Kalshi operates a federally regulated exchange in the United States for event contracts — contracts that pay out depending on whether a stated event happens. The company says its annualized trading volume now exceeds $1 trillion, that it accounts for more than 75% of prediction-market trading volume, and that its non-sports revenue exceeds $1 billion on an annualized basis; those figures are the company's. It plans to use the new capital for product development, its institutional business and international expansion, and, according to reports of its plans, for new products including leveraged event contracts, perpetual futures on individual stocks, and markets based on compute prices.

The valuation prices two things at once. The first is volume: a market that began with political and economic events now runs, by the company's own count, at a trillion-dollar annualized pace, with sports contracts a large part of it. The second is a legal position. Kalshi's sports-related contracts have drawn challenges from state authorities, who allege some offerings amount to unauthorized gambling; Kalshi disputes that reading and operates under federal derivatives regulation through the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. The company's founders, Tarek Mansour and Luana Lopes Lara, started Kalshi in 2018. The round was announced in the week before the November 3 midterm elections, one of the periods when event contracts draw their widest public attention.

item.title: Halloween Spending Reaches a Record $13.5 Billion, and the Candy Bag Costs 71% More Than in 2021
item.description: The National Retail Federation expects record Halloween spending of $13.5 billion, an average of $115.14 per person celebrating. Costumes take $4.4 billion, decorations $4.3 billion and candy $4.1 billion. A 100-piece bag of assorted candy averages $16.96, up 71% since 2021.
item.content:encoded:
Americans are expected to spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, a record, according to the National Retail Federation's annual survey — up from $13.1 billion in 2025, at an average of $115.14 per person celebrating, against $114.45 last year. The survey, conducted by Prosper Insights & Analytics among 7,889 adults from September 1 to 9, splits the spending nearly evenly: costumes $4.4 billion (including $2 billion for adults, $1.5 billion for children and $920 million for pets), decorations $4.3 billion and candy $4.1 billion, with greeting cards adding $0.8 billion. About 74% of consumers plan to celebrate; the most common activities are handing out candy (61%), dressing in costume (50%), and a tie among decorating, carving pumpkins and watching scary movies (42% each). Spider-Man is the leading children's costume, with 4.6 million children planning to wear it.

The candy line carries the price story. A 100-piece bag of assorted Halloween candy averages $16.96 this year, according to a FinanceBuzz study reported by Stacker — up about 3.5% from $16.39 in 2025, and up 71% from $9.91 in 2021. Candy is also the purchase almost nobody skips: 96% of Halloween shoppers plan to buy it, against 78% buying decorations and 71% buying costumes. The arithmetic of the holiday, for the households handing it out tonight, is that the one item bought fresh every year is the one whose price has risen fastest — while the record total is reached by spending slightly more per person across everything else.

item.title: Four Rival AI Labs Agreed to Honor One Line That Opts a Website Out of Training
item.description: OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on Friday they will all honor a single robots.txt token, __usage_ai-training, so a publisher can refuse training use by all four crawlers with one entry. The signal covers training only, not fetching, and does not remove material already collected.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI, Google, Microsoft and Anthropic said on October 30 that they will all honor a single robots.txt policy token, __usage_ai-training, so a website can opt its content out of AI training by all four companies' crawlers with one entry, The Verge reported. The mechanism sits in the file site owners already use to direct crawlers: a User-Agent line naming the token, followed by Disallow or Allow lines that carve out exceptions.

The scope is narrower than the headline suggests, and the reporting states the limits plainly. The token governs training use; it is not a directive about crawling or fetching, so it does not by itself stop a crawler from reading a page for search or for answering a user's question. Updating robots.txt does not remove material already collected into existing datasets or models. The document behind the announcement is an individual IETF Internet-Draft titled "Machine-Readable Training Preference Signal," written by Anthropic's Kevin Kelley and dated October 30, 2026; the IETF's own tracker notes that an individual draft is not endorsed by the IETF and has no formal standing in the standards process.

The timelines differ by company. Anthropic says it has already begun implementing the signal. OpenAI says it aims to implement it in the coming months. Microsoft targets February 1, 2027, and Google says 2027. For publishers, the practical change is administrative: one line in one file, maintained once, replaces separate opt-out mechanisms for each of the four largest Western AI labs — provided the companies implement it on the schedules they have stated, which readers can check against the dates above.

item.title: Foundry Robotics Raised $100 Million to Build a Factory That Switches Products Without Retooling
item.description: Foundry Robotics closed a $100 million Series A led by Marlinspike Partners to expand a 130,000-square-foot factory in Emeryville, California. Its robotic cells are reconfigured by software between products — drones, underwater vehicles, satellites, ground robots and data-center equipment — instead of being rebuilt for each one.
item.content:encoded:
Foundry Robotics has raised $100 million in an oversubscribed Series A round led by Marlinspike Partners, with Khosla Ventures, SE Ventures and Wing VC among the participants. The company will use the money to expand a 130,000-square-foot facility in Emeryville, California, to develop its robotics further and to recruit. Foundry says its manufacturing footprint has increased twentyfold; that figure is the company's.

The company's product is the factory itself. Conventional assembly lines are built for one product and rebuilt — at cost, over months — when the product changes. Foundry's system uses AI-controlled robotic cells that can be reconfigured for different manufacturing tasks, coordinated by its FoundryOS software across the factory floor and cloud systems; data from each assembly run feeds back into the models that run the next one. The company is targeting a specific bottleneck: US defense contractors and industrial hardware producers that need drones, underwater vehicles, satellites, ground robots and data-center equipment in volumes their existing suppliers cannot easily expand to meet.

Foundry was founded by Adarsh Kulkarni and Emmanuel Lamacchia, a former Tesla manufacturing executive. What the announcement does not contain is the operating record: the company has not disclosed production volumes, customer contract values, or independently verified productivity figures, and the coverage of the round notes that absence. The claim being funded is therefore a capacity claim — that software-reconfigurable cells remove the retooling cost that makes small and medium production runs expensive — and the Emeryville expansion is the test of it: a factory twenty times larger either produces across several product lines without retooling, or it becomes a larger version of the conventional plant it set out to replace.

item.title: Five Silicon Qubits Now Share a Single Control Wire
item.description: A RIKEN-led team ran five silicon qubits down one shared microwave line and kept their accuracy at the level error correction requires — attacking the wiring bottleneck that keeps quantum processors small.

item.title: East Antarctica’s Ice Sheet Stayed Stable in 100,000-Year Simulations Even Above 10 Degrees of Warming
item.description: In coupled climate simulations, the largest ice sheet on Earth held up under extreme warming because warmer air delivered it more snow and more cloud cover — while West Antarctica and Greenland, in the same simulations, lost heavily.
